lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the cruciform flower, tetradynamous stamens and replum-bearing fruit as the core mustard-family architecture, then compare directly with Cleomaceae.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module across thirteen project-pool genera
project_scope.note: The pool includes both native and introduced mustards and several legacy generic names. Species-level taxonomy/range stays in separate workflows.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with one flower: usually 4 free sepals + 4 free petals arranged like a cross, then count 6 stamens—typically 4 long and 2 short. Confirm with a silique or silicle whose two valves fall away from a persistent central replum.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly annual, biennial or perennial herbs; leaves usually alternate and without stipules, often forming a basal rosette. Mustard oils commonly produce a pungent odor or taste, but do not rely on tasting plants.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers usually bisexual and radial, commonly in ebracteate racemes. Sepals 4; petals 4 and clawed; stamens usually 6 and tetradynamous—4 longer inner stamens and 2 shorter outer stamens.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Usually a silique or silicle: a 2-valved fruit in which the valves separate from a persistent frame/replum and false septum bearing the seeds.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Four cross-like petals gets attention; 4-long + 2-short stamens and a replum-bearing fruit confirm the family.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: 4-petal cross → tetradynamous stamens → silique/silicle + replum → genus fruit shapes → Cleomaceae contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Mustards are easiest when you stop using flower color and learn the flower-and-fruit machine: four petals, six unequal stamens, then a replum-bearing pod.

steps.title: 1 · See the cross-shaped flower
steps.look_for: Four free petals arranged in a cross, with four sepals beneath.
steps.why_it_matters: The old name Cruciferae literally points to this cross-shaped corolla.

steps.title: 2 · Count 4 long + 2 short stamens
steps.look_for: Six stamens with four conspicuously longer than the other two.
steps.why_it_matters: Tetradynamous stamens are one of the strongest mustard-family confirmation characters.

steps.title: 3 · Open the fruit and find the replum
steps.look_for: Two valves fall away while a central frame/septum remains with the seeds attached.
steps.why_it_matters: The fruit architecture separates Brassicaceae from superficially similar dry pods.

steps.title: 4 · Learn silique vs silicle as shape, not a new fruit type
steps.photo_role: long narrow vs short broad mustard fruits
steps.look_for: Both use the same replum-bearing architecture; 'silique' is elongate, 'silicle' is relatively short/broad.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit shape is extremely useful for narrowing mustard genera.

steps.title: 5 · Use the fruit to enter the genus
steps.look_for: Lepidium and many Draba use shorter silicles; Sisymbrium and Descurainia commonly make long narrow siliques.
steps.why_it_matters: Once family is known, fruit proportions often beat flowers for genus work.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Cleomaceae
comparisons.rule: Brassicaceae usually has a regular cross-shaped 4-petal flower, 6 stamens in a 4-long/2-short pattern, simple/rarely compound leaves without stipules, and a replum-bearing silique/silicle. Local Cleomaceae is often glandular, 3-foliolate, more asymmetric in flower shape, and has 10–20 long exserted stamens.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Fabaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can make pod-like dry fruits, but mustard siliques have two valves separating from a persistent replum; legumes are single-carpel fruits without the mustard replum.

comparisons.title: Brassicaceae vs Caryophyllaceae
comparisons.rule: Caryophyllaceae usually has opposite leaves and 5-merous flowers; Brassicaceae usually has alternate leaves and the 4-petal + tetradynamous-stamen pattern.

visual_lesson.caveat: Not every Brassicaceae flower has all four petals or exactly six stamens, and not every fruit is a textbook dehiscent silique. Use the whole suite rather than one rule.
